notes: The 6532 RIOT provides 128 bytes of RAM, two 8-bit I/O ports and a programmable interval timer. In the 2600 it is selected with A12 = 0 and A7 = 1; A9 = 0 selects the RAM ($0080-$00FF, mirrored at $0180-$01FF) and A9 = 1 selects the I/O and timer area ($0280-$029F and mirrors).

Register decoding (6532 datasheet, Stella): with A2 = 0 the ports are chosen by A1:A0 (00 SWCHA, 01 SWACNT, 10 SWCHB, 11 SWBCNT). With A2 = 1 a read returns INTIM when A0 = 0 and the interrupt flags when A0 = 1; a write with A4 = 1 loads the timer with the divider chosen by A1:A0 (00 TIM1T, 01 TIM8T, 10 TIM64T, 11 T1024T), while a write with A4 = 0 sets up PA7 edge detection (A0 = polarity, A1 = interrupt enable). A3 enables the timer interrupt to the IRQ pin on the real chip.

The timer counts CPU cycles. After loading N with divider D the interrupt flag is set N*D + 1 cycles later, when the counter reads $FF (datasheet example: 52 with divide-by-8 = 417 cycles). From then on it decrements once per cycle whatever the divider, so a late read tells how many cycles ago it expired (value read is the two's complement, minus one). At divider 64 one frame is about 311 ticks (more than the 8-bit range); at 1024 it is about 19 ticks.
Timer expiry plus WSYNC is the classic way to run vertical blank and overscan: wait for INTIM to reach 0, then WSYNC.

Switches are active low where marked: RESET and SELECT read 0 when pressed; the colour/B&W switch reads 1 for colour; difficulty reads 0 for B (amateur) and 1 for A (pro). Joystick bits read 0 when pushed.
The 6507 has no IRQ or NMI pin, so the RIOT interrupt flags are only useful by polling.
Because of partial address decoding RAM and I/O appear at many mirrors; defensive code should use the canonical addresses ($80-$FF, $0280-$0297).

registers.name: SWCHA
registers.summary: Port A data: joysticks, paddle buttons, keypad rows.
registers.description: Read: the state of the 8 port A pins, 0 = active. Bits 7-4 belong to the left port (player 0), bits 3-0 to the right port (player 1). Joystick: bit 7 = P0 right, 6 = left, 5 = down, 4 = up; bit 3 = P1 right, 2 = left, 1 = down, 0 = up. Paddle fire buttons share the port: bit 7 = paddle 0, bit 6 = paddle 1, bit 3 = paddle 2, bit 2 = paddle 3; the paddle positions come through TIA INPT0-INPT3. Write: the output latch for pins that SWACNT configures as outputs; keypad rows and peripherals such as SaveKey/AtariVox use this.
issues: Active low: 0 = pressed. The left port is the high nibble and the right port the low nibble.
Stella models a pin that is an output with a 0 in the latch as pulled low, so a read returns 0 there even when nothing is pressed: only outputs written as 1 leave the pin free.

Keypad controllers: the four rows are driven low through SWCHA output bits (bits 7-4 left, 3-0 right, bit 7 = bottom row of the left keypad, bit 4 = top row) and the columns are read on INPT0, INPT1, INPT4 (left) or INPT2, INPT3, INPT5 (right); the guide asks for about 400 microseconds between the write and the read.
Driving controllers use the up/down bits (4-5 left, 0-1 right) as a two-bit Gray code.
Writing SWCHA with SWACNT = 0 only changes the latch; no pin is driven until the direction register is set.
registers.example:
lda SWCHA
  and #%10000000   ; P0 right
  beq .right

registers.name: SWACNT
registers.description: Port A data direction register: bit = 1 makes the corresponding SWCHA pin an output (driven from the SWCHA latch), 0 makes it an input. The reset value is 0 (all inputs), which is what joystick games use. It can be read back.
issues: Setting outputs with a joystick plugged in fights the controller contacts; it is meant for keypads and peripherals (SaveKey, AtariVox).
A stray write to $0281 (for example a mistyped address) leaves some SWCHA bits driven and breaks joystick reads.

registers.name: SWCHB
registers.description: Console switches, read-only in normal use (SWBCNT = 0). Bit 0 = RESET (0 = pressed). Bit 1 = SELECT (0 = pressed). Bit 3 = colour/B&W: 1 = colour, 0 = B/W. Bit 6 = player 0 (left) difficulty: 0 = B (amateur), 1 = A (pro). Bit 7 = player 1 (right) difficulty, same coding. Bits 2, 4 and 5 are unused (the guide marks them 'not used'; they normally read 1).
issues: RESET and SELECT are active low; the colour switch is 1 = colour.
Bit 3 is the console switch, not a TV-standard detector: there is no register that tells NTSC from PAL.
RESET and SELECT bounce: use the state of the previous frame to detect a press.
The switches are ordinary inputs: the console hardware does not reset the CPU, the program decides what RESET does.

registers.name: SWBCNT
registers.description: Port B data direction register. On the 2600 all port B pins are inputs and the register is left at 0; the guide calls it hardwired as input. Writing 1 to a bit would turn that pin into an output, which has no use for the console switches.
issues: Leave it at 0 so SWCHB reads the switches.
A stray write here (for example an uninitialised pointer hitting $0283) can corrupt switch reads.

registers.name: INTIM
registers.description: Reads the timer. It is loaded by writing TIM1T, TIM8T, TIM64T or T1024T and then decrements once every 1, 8, 64 or 1024 cycles. The interrupt flag is set when it has counted through 0 (the register then reads $FF) and from that moment it decrements once per cycle until a new value is written. Reading INTIM clears the timer flag (TIMINT bit 7); a read at exactly the cycle the flag was set does not clear it.
registers.timing: A value N written with divider D expires N*D + 1 cycles later (datasheet example: 52 with divide-by-8 = 417 cycles). Before expiry the register reads the remaining count, starting at N-1 (the datasheet example reads 51, 50, 49, ...), and it holds 0 for one whole interval (Stella guide) before wrapping to $FF. Programs that wait for INTIM = 0 therefore exit before the flag is set.
issues: After expiry the register counts down by 1 per cycle: the value read is the two's complement of the number of cycles since the wrap, minus one (datasheet).

Typical idiom: write TIM64T, do work, loop on LDA INTIM / BNE, then WSYNC to realign with the beam; the loop exits when INTIM = 0, so the remaining time is under one interval and the WSYNC absorbs it.
Reading INTIM clears the timer flag; reading TIMINT does not touch the timer value.
Unverified: reading INTIM in the very cycle in which it wraps can return either 0 or $FF depending on the emulator; avoid sampling at the boundary or use TIMINT bit 7.
registers.example:
lda #43
  sta TIM64T
.wait:
  lda INTIM
  bne .wait

registers.name: TIMINT
registers.description: Interrupt flag register. Bit 7 = timer flag: set when the timer has counted through 0; cleared by reading INTIM or writing a timer register. Bit 6 = PA7 edge flag: set by the PA7 transition selected with the edge-detect control; cleared by reading this register. The IRQ output is not connected on the 2600, so the flags are only for polling. The other bits read 0.
issues: BIT TIMINT / BMI tests the timer flag without touching the timer value.
The timer flag is cleared by reading INTIM or writing a timer register; the PA7 flag is cleared by reading TIMINT.
The register is also visible at $0287 (A2:A0 = 111); INTIM is also visible at $0286.
PA7 edge detection is rarely used in 2600 software.
The Stella guide does not name this register; TIMINT is the name DASM's vcs.h gave it in version 1.02 (2003), and other tools took it from there. VCSIDE's 2600.h uses that name too.

registers.name: TIM1T
registers.description: Loads the timer with start value N and selects a divider of 1: it decrements every 1 cycle. Maximum interval 255 cycles (about 3.4 scanlines). Writing also clears the timer flag.
issues: After the count passes 0 the timer switches to one decrement per cycle (see INTIM).
A write clears the TIMINT timer flag.

registers.name: TIM8T
registers.description: Loads the timer with start value N and selects a divider of 8: it decrements every 8 cycles. Maximum interval 2040 cycles (just under 27 scanlines). Writing also clears the timer flag.
issues: After the count passes 0 the timer switches to one decrement per cycle (see INTIM).
A write clears the TIMINT timer flag.

registers.name: TIM64T
registers.description: Loads the timer with start value N and selects a divider of 64: it decrements every 64 cycles. Maximum interval 16320 cycles. A 76-cycle scanline is about 1.2 ticks, so this is the usual choice for timing whole sections of a frame. Writing also clears the timer flag.
issues: After the count passes 0 the timer switches to one decrement per cycle (see INTIM).
A write clears the TIMINT timer flag.

Unverified idiom values: TIM64T with 43 for the NTSC vertical blank (2752 cycles vs 37 lines = 2812) and 35-36 for the 30-line overscan are conventional starting points; the exact value depends on the cycles spent before the first line, so derive it from your own code.

registers.name: T1024T
registers.description: Loads the timer with start value N and selects a divider of 1024: it decrements every 1024 cycles. Maximum interval 261120 cycles (about 13 frames). One tick is about 13.5 scanlines. Writing also clears the timer flag.
issues: After the count passes 0 the timer switches to one decrement per cycle (see INTIM).
A write clears the TIMINT timer flag.

registers.name: RAM
registers.summary: 128 bytes of RAM, including the stack.
registers.description: 128 bytes of RAM at $0080-$00FF (zero page), mirrored at $0180-$01FF. The stack lives in page 1, which is the same 128 bytes: with S = $FF the stack top is $01FF = RAM address $FF. Stack and variables compete: variables from $80 upward, stack from $FF downward.
registers.timing: RAM and ROM have the same access time; zero-page forms are shorter.
issues: There is no protection against stack overflow, and 128 bytes are tight.

RAM contents at power-on are undefined (Stella randomises them): initialise $80-$FF at start-up. The usual start-up loop (LDX #0 / TXA / loop with DEX, TXS, PHA) clears the TIA registers and RAM together, but it leaves S wherever the loop ended, so set S explicitly afterwards.
Because of partial decoding the RAM also appears at other mirrors (for example $0480-$04FF); use only $80-$FF and $180-$1FF.
Superchip cartridges add 128 extra bytes in the cartridge address space (see formats.json).
registers.example:
ldx #$FF
  txs        ; stack at top of RAM

registers.name: EDGCTL
registers.description: A write to $0284-$0287 with A4 = 0 configures PA7 edge detection (the datasheet and Stella agree): address bit A0 selects the polarity (0 = falling edge, 1 = rising edge) and bit A1 enables or disables the interrupt from PA7 to the IRQ pin. The data written is ignored. Since IRQ is not connected on the 2600, the only visible effect is bit 6 of TIMINT. Note: on the 2600 the timer registers are at $0294-$0297 (A4 = 1), so $0284-$0287 as write addresses are the edge-detect control.
issues: Rarely used in 2600 software.
The control is carried by the address bits, so STA $0284..$0287 select the mode and the stored value does not matter.
No standard name: neither the Stella guide nor DASM's vcs.h names these addresses; EDGCTL is only the label this documentation uses for them.
